author: maria-lending
title: How a personal loan works
body: A personal loan pays out a fixed amount once and is repaid in equal monthly instalments over a fixed term. Most are unsecured, so the lender prices the risk through the interest rate and decides from the borrower's income, existing debt and credit history.

author: maria-lending
title: Secured versus unsecured loans
body: A secured loan is backed by collateral the lender can claim if the borrower stops paying, such as a car or a home. Because the lender's loss is smaller, secured loans usually carry lower rates and allow larger amounts than unsecured ones.

author: maria-lending
title: Interest rate versus APR
body: The nominal interest rate only covers the cost of borrowing the principal. The annual percentage rate (APR) adds mandatory fees such as origination charges, so APR is the figure to compare when choosing between two loans.

author: maria-lending
title: Amortization schedules explained
body: With an amortizing loan every payment is the same, but its split changes: early payments are mostly interest, later ones mostly principal. An amortization schedule lists, payment by payment, how much goes to each and what balance remains.

author: maria-lending
title: Debt-to-income ratio
body: Lenders divide a borrower's monthly debt payments by gross monthly income to get the debt-to-income ratio (DTI). A lower DTI shows room in the budget for a new payment; many lenders set a maximum as part of underwriting.

author: maria-lending
title: Origination fees and how to spot them
body: An origination fee is charged for processing a loan, often as a percentage of the amount and sometimes deducted from the payout. It raises the APR, so a loan with a lower rate but a high fee can cost more overall.

author: maria-lending
title: Prepaying a loan early
body: Paying extra toward principal shortens the term and reduces total interest. Some contracts include a prepayment penalty that compensates the lender for lost interest, so check the terms before paying a loan off ahead of schedule.

author: maria-lending
title: When refinancing makes sense
body: Refinancing replaces an existing loan with a new one, typically to get a lower rate, a different term or to switch from variable to fixed. It pays off only if the savings exceed the new loan's fees within the time you expect to keep it.

author: maria-lending
title: Auto loans and depreciation
body: An auto loan is secured by the vehicle, which loses value quickly. A large down payment and a shorter term reduce the risk of owing more than the car is worth if it is sold or written off.

author: maria-lending
title: Business term loans
body: A term loan funds a specific investment such as equipment or expansion and is repaid on a fixed schedule. Lenders look at the company's cash flow, financial statements and often require collateral or a personal guarantee from the owners.

author: maria-lending
title: Revolving lines of credit for businesses
body: A business line of credit lets a company draw, repay and draw again up to a limit, paying interest only on what is used. It smooths seasonal gaps in cash flow better than a term loan, which pays out once.

author: maria-lending
title: Balloon payments
body: A balloon loan has small regular payments and a large final payment of the remaining principal. It keeps instalments low but creates refinancing risk if the borrower cannot pay or refinance the balloon when it falls due.

author: maria-lending
title: Loan covenants
body: Covenants are promises in a business loan agreement, such as keeping a minimum interest coverage ratio or not taking on more debt. Breaching one can let the lender demand early repayment or renegotiate terms.

author: tom-credit-risk
title: Probability of default (PD)
body: PD is the likelihood that a borrower fails to meet obligations within a horizon, usually one year. Banks estimate it from internal ratings or scorecards built on historical defaults.

author: tom-credit-risk
title: Loss given default (LGD)
body: LGD is the share of an exposure the bank loses if the borrower defaults, after recoveries from collateral and collections. Well-secured loans have low LGD; unsecured consumer debt has high LGD.

author: tom-credit-risk
title: Exposure at default (EAD)
body: EAD is the amount owed when default happens. For a term loan it is close to the outstanding balance; for credit cards and lines of credit it also includes part of the unused limit that borrowers tend to draw before defaulting.

author: tom-credit-risk
title: Expected loss = PD × LGD × EAD
body: Multiplying the three parameters gives the expected loss of an exposure. Banks price this into interest rates and set provisions against it, while capital covers unexpected losses beyond it.

author: tom-credit-risk
title: Credit scorecards
body: A scorecard turns application data and credit bureau information into points that rank applicants by risk. Lenders choose a cut-off score to approve, refer or decline, trading approval rate against expected defaults.

author: tom-credit-risk
title: Delinquency buckets
body: Banks track overdue loans by days past due: 30, 60, 90 and beyond. Movement between buckets ('roll rates') is an early warning signal; 90 days past due is a common definition of default.

author: tom-credit-risk
title: Charge-offs
body: When a loan is judged uncollectable the bank charges it off, removing it from the balance sheet against the loss allowance. The debt can still be pursued by collections or sold, and recoveries reduce the final loss.

author: tom-credit-risk
title: Loan restructuring for borrowers in difficulty
body: Restructuring changes the terms of a loan, for example extending the term or temporarily reducing payments, to help a struggling borrower avoid default. Regulators require banks to flag these forborne loans and monitor them closely.

author: tom-credit-risk
title: IFRS 9 expected credit loss
body: Under IFRS 9 banks provision for expected losses from day one: 12-month expected loss for performing loans and lifetime expected loss once credit risk has increased significantly or the loan is impaired.

author: tom-credit-risk
title: CECL in the United States
body: The CECL standard requires US lenders to provision for lifetime expected credit losses when a loan is originated, using history, current conditions and reasonable forecasts. It brought provisions forward compared with the earlier incurred-loss model.

author: tom-credit-risk
title: Concentration risk
body: A loan book concentrated in one industry, region or large borrower can suffer correlated losses. Banks set limits by sector and counterparty and hold extra capital where concentration remains.

author: tom-credit-risk
title: Stress testing a loan portfolio
body: A stress test projects defaults and losses under a severe but plausible scenario, such as a recession with rising unemployment and falling house prices. The results show whether capital would stay above regulatory minimums.

author: sam-mortgages
title: Fixed-rate mortgages
body: A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same interest rate for the whole term or a long initial period, so payments are predictable. The borrower pays for that certainty with a rate that is often higher than an introductory variable rate.

author: sam-mortgages
title: Adjustable-rate mortgages
body: An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) starts with a fixed period and then resets periodically to a benchmark rate plus a margin. Caps limit how much the rate can rise per reset and over the loan's life.

author: sam-mortgages
title: Loan-to-value ratio
body: LTV divides the mortgage amount by the property's value. A lower LTV means more equity and less risk for the lender, which is why rates improve and mortgage insurance falls away as LTV drops.

author: sam-mortgages
title: Down payments
body: The down payment is the part of the price paid upfront. A larger one lowers the loan amount, the LTV and often the rate, and can avoid the cost of private mortgage insurance.

author: sam-mortgages
title: Mortgage points
body: Discount points are prepaid interest: paying a percentage of the loan at closing to get a lower rate. They pay off only if you keep the mortgage long enough for the monthly savings to exceed the upfront cost.

author: sam-mortgages
title: Escrow accounts for taxes and insurance
body: Many lenders collect property tax and homeowner's insurance with each mortgage payment and hold it in escrow, paying the bills when due. This protects the collateral and spreads large annual costs over the year.

author: sam-mortgages
title: Mortgage underwriting
body: Underwriters verify income, employment, assets, the credit report and the property appraisal before approving a mortgage. Debt-to-income, loan-to-value and credit score together decide approval and pricing.

author: sam-mortgages
title: Home equity lines of credit
body: A HELOC is a revolving line secured by the home's equity, usually with a variable rate. It offers flexible access to funds, but missed payments put the home at risk because it is the collateral.

author: sam-mortgages
title: Refinancing a mortgage
body: Homeowners refinance to capture a lower rate, change the term or take cash out. Closing costs can be significant, so compare the break-even point with how long you plan to stay in the home.

author: sam-mortgages
title: Foreclosure as a last resort
body: If mortgage payments stop, the lender can eventually take and sell the property to recover the debt. Before that, banks usually offer options such as forbearance or a modification, which cost both sides less.

author: ben-cards
title: What makes up a credit score
body: Common scoring models weigh payment history most, then the amounts owed relative to limits, the length of credit history, the mix of credit types and recent applications. Paying on time every month matters more than anything else.

author: ben-cards
title: Credit utilization
body: Utilization is the share of available revolving credit you are using. Keeping balances well below limits, for example under 30 percent, tends to support a better score than running cards close to the limit.

author: ben-cards
title: Hard and soft inquiries
body: A hard inquiry happens when you apply for credit and can lower a score slightly for a while. Soft inquiries, such as checking your own report or pre-approval offers, do not affect the score.

author: ben-cards
title: Reading your credit report
body: A credit report lists accounts, balances, payment history and inquiries held by a credit bureau. Check it regularly and dispute errors, because lenders and scores rely on it.

author: ben-cards
title: How credit card interest works
body: Card interest is charged on balances carried past the due date, usually calculated daily from the APR. Paying the full statement balance each month avoids interest on purchases entirely.

author: ben-cards
title: The grace period on purchases
body: The grace period is the time between the statement date and the due date during which purchases accrue no interest if the previous balance was paid in full. Carrying a balance usually removes the grace period on new purchases.

author: ben-cards
title: Minimum payments
body: The minimum payment keeps an account current but mostly covers interest. Paying only the minimum on a large balance can take years and cost far more than the original purchases.

author: ben-cards
title: Revolving versus instalment credit
body: Revolving credit, like a card, has a limit you can reuse; instalment credit, like a car loan, pays out once and is repaid on a schedule. Scoring models consider having both types responsibly as a positive.

author: ben-cards
title: Secured credit cards
body: A secured card is backed by a cash deposit that usually becomes the credit limit. It helps people with no or damaged credit history build a record of on-time payments.

author: ben-cards
title: Credit builder loans
body: With a credit builder loan the bank holds the borrowed amount in a savings account while the borrower makes payments; the money is released at the end. The on-time payments are reported to the bureaus.

author: ben-cards
title: Balance transfers
body: A balance transfer moves card debt to a new card, often at a low introductory rate. A transfer fee applies, and the remaining balance reverts to the regular APR when the promotion ends.

author: raj-retail
title: Debit cards versus credit cards
body: A debit card spends money already in your account; a credit card borrows from the issuer and bills you later. Debit avoids debt and interest, while credit cards build credit history and offer stronger dispute protections in many countries.

author: raj-retail
title: How a checking account works
body: A checking (current) account holds money for everyday payments: card purchases, transfers, direct debits and cash withdrawals. It pays little or no interest because the balance is meant to be spent.

author: raj-retail
title: Overdrafts
body: An overdraft lets the account go below zero up to an agreed limit. It is a short-term loan with fees or interest, useful for emergencies but expensive as a regular habit.

author: raj-retail
title: Insufficient funds and returned payments
body: If a payment is presented without enough money and no overdraft, the bank may return it unpaid and charge a fee. Low-balance alerts and a buffer in the account prevent most of these charges.

author: raj-retail
title: PIN and signature debit
body: A PIN debit transaction is authorised with the card's PIN and usually settles directly against the account; signature or contactless debit runs over the card network like a credit transaction. Both draw on the same balance.

author: raj-retail
title: ATM withdrawals and fees
body: Withdrawing from your own bank's ATMs is usually free; other operators may charge a fee, and your bank may add its own. Daily withdrawal limits protect the account if the card is stolen.

author: raj-retail
title: Savings accounts and APY
body: A savings account pays interest on deposits. The annual percentage yield (APY) includes compounding, so it is the right number to compare between accounts.

author: raj-retail
title: Compound interest
body: Compounding means interest earns interest. The more often it is credited and the longer money stays invested, the faster the balance grows, which is why starting to save early matters.

author: raj-retail
title: Certificates of deposit
body: A certificate of deposit (term deposit) pays a fixed rate for locking money away for a set period. Withdrawing early usually costs a penalty, so match the term to when you will need the cash.

author: raj-retail
title: Deposit insurance
body: Deposit insurance schemes protect depositors up to a limit per bank if the bank fails. Knowing the limit matters for large balances, which can be spread across several insured banks.

author: raj-retail
title: Building an emergency fund
body: An emergency fund covers several months of essential expenses in an easily accessible savings account. It keeps unexpected costs from turning into card debt or overdraft fees.

author: aisha-payments
title: Card networks and the four-party model
body: A card payment involves the cardholder, the issuing bank, the merchant and the merchant's acquiring bank, connected by a card network. The network routes authorisations and settles funds between issuer and acquirer.

author: aisha-payments
title: Authorisation, clearing and settlement
body: At the till the issuer authorises the payment and places a hold; later the transaction is cleared and settled between banks. That is why a purchase can show as pending before it posts.

author: aisha-payments
title: Interchange fees
body: Interchange is the fee the acquirer pays the issuer on each card transaction, set by the networks or capped by regulation in some regions. It is the largest part of what merchants pay to accept cards.

author: aisha-payments
title: Chargebacks
body: A chargeback reverses a card payment after the cardholder disputes it with the issuer, for example for fraud or goods not received. The merchant can contest it with evidence; frequent chargebacks raise its costs.

author: aisha-payments
title: Direct debits
body: A direct debit authorises a company to collect variable amounts from your account, such as utility bills. Schemes like SEPA Direct Debit give the payer the right to refund within a set period.

author: aisha-payments
title: ACH transfers
body: ACH is the US batch network for direct deposits, bill payments and transfers between banks. It is cheap and reliable, and same-day ACH has shortened what used to take one or two business days.

author: aisha-payments
title: Wire transfers and SWIFT
body: A wire moves money between banks individually and quickly, domestically or cross-border. International wires use SWIFT messages, may pass through correspondent banks and are hard to reverse once sent.

author: aisha-payments
title: Instant payments
body: Instant payment schemes such as SEPA Instant, FedNow and many national systems settle account-to-account transfers in seconds, around the clock. Speed helps customers but also gives fraudsters less time to be stopped.

author: aisha-payments
title: Card tokenization
body: Tokenization replaces the card number with a token tied to one device or merchant. Mobile wallets and stored cards use tokens, so a breached merchant database does not expose real card numbers.

author: aisha-payments
title: Open banking APIs
body: Open banking lets customers authorise licensed third parties to read account data or initiate payments through bank APIs. It enables budgeting apps and account-to-account payments without sharing passwords.

author: aisha-payments
title: Strong customer authentication
body: Strong customer authentication requires two of: something you know, something you have and something you are. European rules require it for most online payments, using protocols such as 3-D Secure for cards.

author: nina-fraud
title: Card-not-present fraud
body: When stolen card details are used online, the card is not present to check. Merchants and issuers counter it with 3-D Secure, device fingerprinting, address checks and risk scoring of each transaction.

author: nina-fraud
title: Account takeover
body: In an account takeover, a criminal gains access to a customer's online banking, often through phishing or reused passwords. Unusual logins, new devices and changed contact details are key warning signs.

author: nina-fraud
title: Authorised push payment scams
body: In an APP scam the customer is tricked into sending money themselves, for example to a fake 'safe account'. Because the customer authorised it, prevention relies on warnings, confirmation of payee and delays on risky transfers.

author: nina-fraud
title: Transaction monitoring with risk scores
body: Fraud systems score each transaction in real time from features such as amount, merchant, location and device, combining rules and machine-learning models. High scores trigger a decline, a step-up check or a review.

author: nina-fraud
title: Phishing and social engineering
body: Most fraud starts with persuasion, not hacking: a call, text or email pretending to be the bank. Banks never ask for full PINs or passwords, and customers should call back on the number printed on their card.

author: nina-fraud
title: Synthetic identity fraud
body: Synthetic identities combine real and invented data to create a person who does not exist, who then builds credit before 'busting out' with maxed-out cards and loans. Strong identity verification at onboarding is the main defence.

author: nina-fraud
title: Money mules
body: Money mules move stolen funds through their own accounts, sometimes unknowingly through fake job offers. Spotting mule accounts links fraud prevention with anti-money-laundering monitoring.

author: li-compliance
title: Know your customer (KYC)
body: KYC means verifying a customer's identity and understanding the purpose of the relationship when an account is opened, and keeping that information current. It is the foundation of fighting fraud and money laundering.

author: li-compliance
title: Customer due diligence and enhanced due diligence
body: Standard due diligence applies to most customers; higher-risk ones, such as politically exposed persons or complex structures, get enhanced due diligence with more evidence and senior approval.

author: li-compliance
title: Anti-money laundering basics
body: Money laundering disguises criminal proceeds through placement, layering and integration. Banks fight it with KYC, transaction monitoring, record keeping and reporting suspicious activity to authorities.

author: li-compliance
title: Suspicious activity reports
body: When staff or monitoring systems find activity that may involve laundering or fraud, the bank files a suspicious activity report with the financial intelligence unit. Tipping off the customer is prohibited.

author: li-compliance
title: Sanctions screening
body: Banks screen customers and payments against sanctions lists and must block or freeze matches. Fuzzy name matching produces many false positives, which analysts clear with additional data such as date of birth.

author: li-compliance
title: Beneficial ownership
body: For company accounts, banks identify the natural persons who ultimately own or control the business. Hidden ownership through shell companies is a classic laundering technique.

author: li-compliance
title: Data protection in banking
body: Banks process sensitive personal and financial data and must limit collection, secure storage and access, and honour customer rights under laws such as GDPR. Open banking adds explicit consent for sharing data.

author: li-compliance
title: Fair lending and affordability
body: Lending rules require banks to assess whether a borrower can afford a loan and to avoid discrimination in approvals and pricing. Models used in credit decisions must be explainable and monitored for bias.

author: olga-treasury
title: Net interest margin
body: Net interest margin is the difference between what a bank earns on loans and investments and what it pays on deposits and borrowing, relative to earning assets. It is the core of a traditional bank's profit.

author: olga-treasury
title: How central bank rates reach customers
body: When the central bank changes its policy rate, interbank and market rates follow, and banks reprice variable-rate loans and, more slowly, deposit rates. Fixed-rate loans are affected only when they are renewed or refinanced.

author: olga-treasury
title: Interest rate risk in the banking book
body: If assets and liabilities reprice at different times, changing rates move a bank's earnings and economic value. Treasury measures the gap and hedges it, for example with interest rate swaps.

author: olga-treasury
title: Asset-liability management
body: ALM coordinates the bank's balance sheet: the maturities of loans and funding, interest rate exposure and liquidity. Decisions are taken by an ALCO committee within limits set by the board.

author: olga-treasury
title: Liquidity coverage ratio
body: The LCR requires banks to hold enough high-quality liquid assets to cover estimated net cash outflows over a 30-day stress period. It protects against sudden deposit withdrawals.

author: olga-treasury
title: Net stable funding ratio
body: The NSFR requires long-term assets such as mortgages to be funded with stable sources such as long-term debt and sticky deposits, limiting reliance on short-term wholesale funding.

author: olga-treasury
title: Capital adequacy
body: Regulators require banks to hold capital, mainly common equity, against risk-weighted assets so losses can be absorbed without failing. Riskier loans carry higher risk weights and need more capital.

author: olga-treasury
title: Deposits as a funding source
body: Retail deposits are usually the cheapest and most stable funding for a bank, especially when insured. Banks still model how quickly different deposit types could leave in stress.

author: olga-treasury
title: The yield curve and lending
body: The yield curve plots interest rates by maturity. Banks borrow short and lend long, so a steep curve helps margins while an inverted one squeezes them and often signals slower growth.

author: olga-treasury
title: Interbank lending
body: Banks lend each other reserves overnight and for short terms to manage daily liquidity. Benchmark rates such as SOFR and €STR are derived from these money markets and feed into loan pricing.

author: eva-education
title: Building a monthly budget
body: List income after tax, then fixed costs, debt payments and savings, and only then flexible spending. A budget that pays yourself first makes saving automatic rather than whatever is left over.

author: eva-education
title: Paying off debt: avalanche or snowball
body: The avalanche method pays the highest-interest debt first and saves the most money; the snowball method clears the smallest balance first for quick wins. Either works if extra payments continue.

author: eva-education
title: Good debt and bad debt
body: Borrowing that builds lasting value at a reasonable cost, such as an affordable mortgage or education, differs from high-interest debt for consumption. The rate, the purpose and the ability to repay decide which it is.

author: eva-education
title: How to compare loan offers
body: Compare the APR, the total amount repayable, the term, fees and flexibility such as penalty-free overpayments. The lowest monthly payment is often the most expensive loan overall.

author: eva-education
title: Improving a low credit score
body: Pay every bill on time, reduce card balances, avoid many applications at once and keep old accounts open. Scores recover gradually as negative entries age.

author: eva-education
title: Protecting yourself from banking scams
body: Treat urgency as a red flag, never move money to a 'safe account', and verify requests through the official app or phone number. Report suspected fraud to the bank immediately; speed improves the chance of recovery.

author: eva-education
title: Choosing the right bank account
body: Look at monthly fees, overdraft terms, ATM access, interest on balances, the quality of the app and deposit insurance. Many people use one account for bills and another for savings.
